title: What It Took to Survive Life on a Pirate Ship in 1718
fullText: The Caribbean 1718 A merchant captain stands on the deck of his sugar transport, watching the horizon. He sees the sails first, then the flag. Before any cannon fires, before any boarding hook is thrown, he orders his crew to surrender. The pirate ship is still 100 yard away. In the ship's log, he writes one sentence to explain his decision. He doesn't write about the weapons. He doesn't write about the size of the crew. He writes that their unbearable stench had already begun to board his ship from a 100 yards away. The pirates didn't need to attack. The smell was the warning. That is what a pirate ship in the golden age of piracy actually was. Not the swashbuckling treasure hunting adventure Hollywood gave us. Something far stranger, far more brutal, and in some ways far more revolutionary than the world that was hunting them down. This is the documented reality of life on a pirate ship between 1680 and 1730. the men who lived it, what they ate, how they slept, who they really were. This is what it actually took to live on that ship. Being a pirate was never a child's dream. It was a choice made by men who had run out of better choices. When authorities captured pirate ships in the early 1700s, [music] they often found something they didn't expect. Former Royal Navy officers working alongside escaped slaves. Disgraced doctors next to former tax collectors. One arrest record from 1721 listed a crew of 48 men from 12 different nations. The pirate ships of the golden age were perhaps the most diverse workplaces in the entire world. Not because their crews believed [music] in equality as a principle, because they couldn't afford to be picky. Merchant ships paid almost nothing and treated their sailors like animals. The Royal [music] Navy paid better, but use flogging as a daily management tool. For a man with no land, no family, no name worth using, a pirate ship was often the least bad option available. Approximately 25 to 30% of golden age pirates [music] were black. Many were escaped slaves who had been working on plantations. Some rose to leadership positions. A few ended up commanding their own ships in an era when slavery was legal across most of the Caribbean. [music] On a pirate ship, the question of where you were born mattered less than whether you could pull your weight. A reformed pirate writing in 1704 said it plainly, "The sea welcomes all who dare to sail it. Just as pirates accept anyone who can pull their weight, regardless of birthplace or beliefs, women were rarer, but not unheard of. Anne Bonnie and Mary Reed are the most famous, but they weren't the only ones. Court records from the 1720s mention several others. During one skirmish, as most of the male crew hid below deck, a female pirate stood on the upper deck and screamed at her own crew mates to come up and fight if they truly considered themselves men. This was the labor pool. The men and a few women who had nowhere else to go. The ship was built around them. Here is the thing about pirate ships that nobody teaches you in school. They invented modern labor law. Every man who joined a golden age pirate crew was required to sign a document called the articles. These were written agreements that laid out exactly how the ship would be run, how much each man would be paid, what he would receive if he was injured, what punishments existed for breaking the rules. Every man signed before the ship sailed. This was revolutionary. In 1718, no merchant vessel on Earth had anything like it. Sailors on Royal Navy ships had no contract. Workers in factories [music] had no contract. The articles were the first written workplace agreements in maritime history and possibly the first written workplace agreements anywhere in the modern world. And they were created not by governments or by employers but by the workers themselves. The compensation clauses were the most striking part. A typical article stated that if any man lost a joint in the time of an engagement, he would receive 400 pieces of eight. For a limb, 800. To understand what that means, you have to understand what a working man earned in 1718. A skilled laborer on land might make 60 to 80 pieces of eight in an entire year of honest work. 800 pieces of eight for a lost arm was the equivalent of 10 years of legitimate wages. The pirates had created the first disability insurance plan in maritime history and the payouts were better than most modern jobs. The captain himself was elected. He could be voted out during quiet times. Decisions about which ships to attack were taken by vote. Every man with an equal voice regardless of rank or experience. In 1718, a famous pirate captain wanted to engage a heavily armed merchant vessel. His crew voted against it. He respected the decision. on a Royal Navy ship. Questioning the captain that way could get you whipped to the bone. But don't mistake this democracy for kindness. The same articles that paid for your lost arm could also get you marooned on a deserted island for stealing from a shipmate. Below decks, the pirate democracy ended. There was no vote about what the ship smelled like. The lower decks of a golden age pirate ship were dark, constantly damp, crowded with bodies, gear, livestock, and rats. Always rats. The wooden hull had no insulation, no ventilation, and no plumbing. Whatever happened below decks stayed below decks, and in the heat of the Caribbean, it decomposed [music] for days. Rats outnumbered the crew. They lived in the rope coils, in the cargo hold, in the seams of the food barrels. They chewed through ration sacks. They spread disease. There were no bathrooms. The head was an area at the front of the ship where a man could hang precariously over the bow sprit, suspended above the sea, and relieve himself directly into the water below. In rough weather, this simple necessity became a deathdeying act. Men were occasionally swept off and lost. Washing rarely happened. Most pirates went months without a proper bath. Some would strip down during rainstorms to rinse off sea salt. Others used seaater and sand to scrub their skin raw. The resulting body odor was so universal that contemporary pirate accounts didn't even mention it. It was simply the background condition of their existence. This is why the 1718 merchant captain surrendered from a 100 yards away. Sleep happened in canvas hammocks slung in cramped quarters below decks. Hammocks were strung roughly 14 in apart, close enough that you could feel your neighbor's breath. Privacy did not exist. Personal space extended only as far as one's small wooden chest, which contained every earthly possession a pirate owned. The watches ran in 4hour rotations. Half the crew worked while the other half slept. You drifted off to the sound of rats moving through the timbers, the snoring of 40 men packed shoulderto-shoulder, and the constant creaking of a wooden hull twisting in Atlantic swells. Then someone kicked your hammock and your watch began. 4 hours of work, 4 hours of sleep for months at a stretch. And the food was the next problem. The food was its own kind of torture. The staple of every pirate ship was hard attack, a brick of flour and water baked twice until it was hard enough to break teeth. By the second week of a voyage, the heart attack was usually infested with weevils. By the second month, it had to be soaked in beer or rum just to be edible. Pirates learned to eat in the dark so they didn't have to see what they were swallowing. Salt pork and salt beef formed the rest of the diet. Boiled to mush in a small galley fire, salted to the point of being almost inedible for any modern pallet. Cooks rotated stolen spices to mask the taste of meat that was often half rotten by the time it was served. On lucky days, fresh fish, captured turtle, or stolen plantation fruit supplemented the rations. The bigger problem wasn't food. [music] It was water. Fresh water stored in wooden barrels turned foul within days. [music] Algae bloomed inside the casks. The water acquired a putrid taste and could carry disease that killed a crew faster than any battle. By the end of the first week of a voyage, the drinking water on most ships was undrinkable. This is why pirates drank rum. Not because they loved it, because their water had gone bad and rum hadn't. Some crews drank weak [music] beer instead, but the principle was the same. Alcohol kept longer than water. Alcohol couldn't be contaminated. Alcohol kept men alive on voyages that water alone could not. And without fresh fruit, scurvy stalked every voyage. Vitamin C deficiency made gums rot, teeth fall out, old wounds reopen. Smart captains raided plantations for citrus as eagerly as they raided merchant ships for gold. the crews that didn't lost men slowly, [music] painfully, week after week, to a disease that a single barrel of lemons would have prevented. Now, stop for a second and ask yourself something honestly. Salt pork, weevil [music] biscuits, rum, because the water is poison. Could you do this voyage? Drop your answer in the comments before we get to the part that's actually dangerous. The dangerous part wasn't the food. The dangerous part was the hunt. Hollywood gave us pirate ships sailing the open seas, attacking everything that moved. The reality was the opposite. The average pirate ship in 1718 might spot a viable target once every week or two. Atlantic shipping lanes were vast. Random encounters were rare. Successful piracy [music] was a chess game. Information was the most valuable cargo on a pirate ship. Before setting sail, crews relied on a web of informants in every Caribbean port. [music] Corrupt harbor officials sold shipping schedules. Tavern [music] keepers passed on tips about valuable cargo. Even legitimate merchants sometimes supplied information in exchange for a share of the take. Court records from the 1720s revealed that nearly 20% of captured pirates implicated reputable businessmen as their secret partners. One pirate on the morning he was hanged in 1722 made a remark that has never been forgotten. He said the only real difference between pirates and merchants was that pirates openly [music] admitted to theft. The judge was not amused. The merchant partners watching from the crowd as respectable citizens said nothing at all. The [music] maps mattered as much as the informants. Pirate charts were not the buried treasure maps of fiction. They were detailed navigational charts showing shipping lanes, seasonal wind patterns [music] and choke points. The narrow passages where shipping was forced to converge. The windward passage between Cuba and Hispanola. The waters of Charleston, the straits near the Bahamas. By positioning themselves at these maritime bottlenecks, [music] pirate crews increased their odds of encounters from once a fortnight to nearly daily. The ideal target was specific. A pirate captain in 1719 described it in his journal as fat of cargo and thin of courage. [music] A heavily laden merchant ship with minimal armorament. Sugar from the Caribbean in August. [music] slave ships heading to the Americas in spring, spice ships returning from Asia in early autumn. When their crews had been at sea for months and were too tired to fight, when the pirate ship found one, it sailed under a false friendly flag until the last possible moment. Then it raised the black flag. The black flag was an invitation to surrender. Most merchant captains accepted it. Pirates preferred surrender to combat. A ship sunk in battle was a ship lost. A ship damaged in battle was a profit ruined. The whole point of piracy was capture, not destruction. So pirates worked hard to make their reputation more terrifying than their actual attack. This is where the costumes came from. Edward Teach, better known as Blackbeard, tied slow burning fuses into his beard and lit them before boarding, surrounding his face with demonic smoke. Other captains painted themselves with blood red dyes. They shouted in multiple languages at once, creating an impression of wild, uncontrollable fury. The goal was to make the merchant crew surrender before a single blow was struck. If surrender didn't come, the boarding action began. Grappling hooks, iron claws on ropes, were hurled across to lock the two ships together. escape became impossible. Pirates swarmed across using boarding planks or simply swinging over on ropes. They carried cutlasses, shorter and broader than military swords, brutally effective in cramped shipboard conditions. They carried multiple loaded flint lock pistols stuffed into sashes. Not because the pistols were accurate, but because a pirate could fire six times before a defender fired once. They carried boarding axes that could split a defender's skull or break down a locked cabin door with equal efficiency. Some carried glass grenades, bottles filled with gunpowder and nails to clear an enemy deck before climbing aboard. The fighting itself was almost always short. Most shipboard battles lasted less than 15 minutes. The pirate goal was not a battle. It was an overwhelming impression of inevitable defeat. If the merchant crew believed resistance was futile, they would surrender quickly, which was good for everyone. After the fight came the bargain. Captured sailors were separated from their officers and offered a choice. Join the pirate crew or wait in the cargo hold until the next port. Roughly 35% of golden age pirates began their careers exactly this way. As merchant sailors captured in a boarding action who took the offered place over the alternative, the pirate crew, just like the ship's articles, grew through volunteers. But every pirate career ended. The average golden age pirates active career was just 2 to 3 years. The end usually came in one of three ways. Death in battle, capture by a naval patrol, or most often, betrayal by his own crew. Nearly 60% of pirate captains captured during the Golden Age were turned in by their own crewmen. The famous Brotherhood, the loyalty that pirates claimed and celebrated, collapsed almost completely when the threat of a noose appeared. The reward [music] money offered for a captain's head was enough to buy out the loyalty of men who had voted for him months before. Honor, it turned out, had its limits when the gallows were waiting. For pirates who refused to fight [music] bravely, refused to share the plunder fairly, or stole from a shipmate, justice was internal and immediate. The standard punishment was marooning. dropped on a deserted island with a single bottle of water, a single pistol, and one shot inside it. No appeals. The sentence was carried out the same day it was decided for pirates captured by naval patrols. The punishments were designed to send a message. The trials were swift. The first dedicated piracy courts could complete an entire cruise trial in under 6 hours with conviction rates approaching 95%. The executions that followed were public spectacles. Captured pirates were hanged at harbor entrances. Their bodies were left in iron cages until three tides had washed over them. Then they were tarred and displayed in prominent locations around port cities as warnings to anyone considering the same career. Walking the plank, by the way, was almost entirely a Victorian invention. Real pirates simply threw troublemakers overboard. Less dramatic, but faster. Buried treasure was equally imaginary. Only two authenticated cases of buried pirate treasure have ever [music] been documented. Real pirates spent their plunder within days. The romantic version came later. The reality was the rope. The golden age of piracy lasted less than 50 years. By the 1730s, the Royal Navy and the colonial governments had hunted most of the famous crews to the gallows. The black flags came down. The merchant traffic resumed. [music] What the pirates left behind was almost nothing in treasure. Most of their gold was spent or lost. The legends grew, but the gold was already gone. What they did leave behind was harder to measure. Workplace contracts that workers themselves had written, disability insurance for laborers, [music] democratic voting on group decisions, compensation for injury on the job. Ideas that the rest of the world wouldn't catch up to for almost 200 years. That is the real legacy of the pirate ship. Not the parrot, not the patch. The idea that even men with nothing left could write their own rules. If you want more stories like this, subscribe to Worlds Before Us. We'll see you in the next one.
